chapter_text:
CHAPTER 16 - ANGLES IN A CIRCLE

Introduction

A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre). Many beautiful and useful facts follow simply from this definition, especially facts about the ANGLES that arise inside a circle. In this chapter we study the angles that chords, arcs and the centre create, and we develop a small set of theorems that let us find unknown angles quickly. These results - the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angles in the same segment, the angle in a semicircle, and the properties of a cyclic quadrilateral - form the toolkit of 'angle chasing' that appears throughout geometry.

16.1 SOME BASIC TERMS

Recall a few terms. A CHORD is a line segment joining two points on the circle. A DIAMETER is a chord that passes through the centre; it is the longest chord and equals twice the radius. An ARC is a part of the circle between two points on it. Any chord divides the circle into two arcs: the shorter is the MINOR arc and the longer is the MAJOR arc. A chord also divides the interior of the circle into two SEGMENTS - the minor segment (on the side of the minor arc) and the major segment (on the side of the major arc). A SEMICIRCLE is either half of the circle cut off by a diameter.

An ANGLE SUBTENDED BY AN ARC (or by a chord) at a point means the angle formed at that point by the two lines drawn from the point to the two endpoints of the arc (or chord). For example, if PQ is a chord and A is any other point, then angle PAQ is the angle subtended by chord PQ at the point A.

16.2 CENTRAL ANGLE AND INSCRIBED ANGLE

A CENTRAL ANGLE (or angle at the centre) is an angle whose vertex is at the centre O of the circle and whose two arms are radii. The central angle subtended by an arc AB is simply angle AOB, where O is the centre. Because the two arms are radii of equal length, the central angle is a direct measure of how 'big' the arc is: an arc that is one quarter of the circle subtends a central angle of 90 degrees, a semicircular arc subtends 180 degrees, and the whole circle corresponds to 360 degrees.

An INSCRIBED ANGLE (or angle at the circumference) is an angle whose vertex lies ON the circle and whose two arms are chords of the circle. If A and B are the endpoints of an arc and P is any other point on the remaining part of the circle, then angle APB is the inscribed angle subtended by arc AB at P. The point P is said to lie on the arc REMAINING after we remove arc AB; the inscribed angle 'looks at' the chord AB from the far side.

The whole chapter revolves around comparing these two kinds of angle for the SAME arc.

16.3 THE ANGLE-AT-CENTRE THEOREM

THEOREM (Angle at the Centre). The angle subtended by an arc of a circle at the centre is DOUBLE the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

In symbols, if arc AB subtends angle AOB at the centre O and angle APB at a point P on the major arc, then angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.

Proof (outline). Join P to the centre O and extend PO to a point Q on the far side, so that PQ passes through O. In triangle OAP, the two sides OA and OP are radii, so OA = OP and the triangle is isosceles; therefore angle OAP = angle OPA. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so the exterior angle AOQ = angle OAP + angle OPA = 2 x angle OPA. Similarly, in triangle OBP we have OB = OP, so angle OBP = angle OPB, and the exterior angle BOQ = 2 x angle OPB. Adding, angle AOQ + angle BOQ = 2(angle OPA + angle OPB), that is angle AOB = 2 x angle APB. (When arc AB is a major arc the corresponding reflex angle at the centre is used, and the same doubling relation holds.)

This single theorem is the parent of almost every other result in the chapter.

16.4 ANGLES IN THE SAME SEGMENT

THEOREM. Angles in the same segment of a circle are EQUAL.

Suppose chord AB divides the circle, and P and Q are two points both lying on the same (major) arc - that is, both in the same segment. Then angle APB = angle AQB. The reason is immediate from the Angle-at-Centre theorem: each of these inscribed angles is half of the SAME central angle AOB. Since both equal (1/2) x angle AOB, they must be equal to each other. So no matter where you place the vertex on a given arc, the angle it makes looking at a fixed chord stays the same.

CONVERSE. If a line segment AB subtends equal angles at two points P and Q lying on the same side of AB, then the four points A, B, P, Q are CONCYCLIC (they lie on one circle). This converse is the standard test for four points lying on a circle.

16.5 ANGLE IN A SEMICIRCLE

THEOREM. The angle in a semicircle is a RIGHT ANGLE (90 degrees).

Let AB be a diameter, O the centre, and P any point on the circle other than A or B. Then angle APB = 90 degrees. This is a special case of the Angle-at-Centre theorem: the arc AB (a semicircle) subtends a straight angle of 180 degrees at the centre (since AOB is a straight line through O). The inscribed angle APB is half of this, namely (1/2) x 180 = 90 degrees. So the diameter of a circle always 'sees' a right angle from any point on the circle.

CONVERSE. If AB is a fixed segment and P is a point such that angle APB = 90 degrees, then P lies on the circle having AB as diameter. Equivalently, the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is a diameter of the triangle's circumscribed circle, and its midpoint is the circumcentre - equidistant from all three vertices.

16.6 CYCLIC QUADRILATERALS

A QUADRILATERAL whose four vertices all lie on a single circle is called a CYCLIC QUADRILATERAL (the vertices are said to be concyclic). Its four sides are chords of the circle.

THEOREM. The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are SUPPLEMENTARY - they add up to 180 degrees.

Let ABCD be a cyclic quadrilateral with centre O. Consider the pair of opposite angles at B and D. Angle A + angle C = 180 degrees, and likewise angle B + angle D = 180 degrees. Proof (outline). Angle A (that is angle DAB) is the inscribed angle standing on arc BCD, so it equals half the central angle for that arc. Angle C (angle BCD) is the inscribed angle standing on the other arc BAD, so it equals half the central angle for that arc. The two central angles together make a full turn of 360 degrees, so the two inscribed angles together make half of 360, that is 180 degrees. Hence angle A + angle C = 180, and similarly angle B + angle D = 180.

CONVERSE. If a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic. This is the standard test for a quadrilateral to be inscribed in a circle.

EXTERIOR ANGLE PROPERTY. If one side of a cyclic quadrilateral is produced (extended), the EXTERIOR angle so formed equals the INTERIOR angle at the opposite vertex. For example, if side AB of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD is produced to a point E, then the exterior angle CBE equals the interior opposite angle ADC. This follows because the exterior angle CBE = 180 - angle ABC (linear pair), and angle ABC + angle ADC = 180 (opposite angles supplementary), so angle CBE = angle ADC.

16.7 WORKED ANGLE-CHASING EXAMPLES

Example 1. O is the centre of a circle and A, B, P are points on it. If angle AOB = 80 degrees (central angle on minor arc AB), find angle APB where P is on the major arc. Solution: angle APB = (1/2) x angle AOB = (1/2) x 80 = 40 degrees.

Example 2. In a circle, chord AB subtends angle APB = 35 degrees at a point P on the major arc. Find the central angle angle AOB. Solution: angle AOB = 2 x angle APB = 2 x 35 = 70 degrees.

Example 3. AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle. If angle ABC = 55 degrees, find angle BAC. Solution: angle ACB is the angle in a semicircle = 90 degrees. In triangle ABC the angles sum to 180, so angle BAC = 180 - 90 - 55 = 35 degrees.

Example 4. ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle A = 95 degrees and angle B = 70 degrees. Find angles C and D. Solution: opposite angles are supplementary, so angle C = 180 - angle A = 180 - 95 = 85 degrees, and angle D = 180 - angle B = 180 - 70 = 110 degrees.

Example 5. In a circle, points P and Q lie on the same arc over chord AB. If angle APB = 48 degrees, what is angle AQB? Solution: angles in the same segment are equal, so angle AQB = 48 degrees.

SUMMARY

- A central angle has its vertex at the centre; an inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle. Both may stand on the same arc.
- Angle-at-Centre theorem: the angle an arc subtends at the centre is twice the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining circle (angle AOB = 2 x angle APB).
- Angles in the same segment are equal, because each is half of the same central angle. The converse gives a concyclic-points test.
- The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees, because the diameter subtends 180 degrees at the centre. Its converse locates a right-angle vertex on a circle with the hypotenuse as diameter.
- In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are supplementary (sum 180 degrees); the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle. The converses are tests for concyclicity.
- Angle chasing combines these theorems with the triangle angle-sum (180 degrees) and the isosceles-triangle property of radii to find unknown angles.

topics.description: The idea of an angle subtended by an arc or chord; a central angle (vertex at the centre, arms are radii) versus an inscribed angle (vertex on the circle, arms are chords); minor and major arcs and segments.

topics.name: Angle at Centre is Double the Angle at Circumference
topics.description: The Angle-at-Centre theorem: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining circle, with its isosceles-triangle proof.

topics.name: Angles in the Same Segment
topics.description: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal because each is half of the same central angle; the converse test for concyclic points.

topics.name: Angle in a Semicircle
topics.description: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90 degrees) as a special case of the Angle-at-Centre theorem; the converse placing a right-angle vertex on a circle with the hypotenuse as diameter.

topics.name: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
topics.description: A quadrilateral inscribed in a circle; opposite angles are supplementary (sum 180 degrees); the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle; the converse tests for a cyclic quadrilateral.

topics.name: Angle-Chasing Problems in Circles
topics.description: Combining the circle theorems with the triangle angle-sum and isosceles-radius facts to compute unknown angles and to prove further results.

chapter_summary.title: Angles in a Circle - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter studies the angles that arcs, chords and the centre of a circle create. It builds a small toolkit of theorems - the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angles in the same segment, the angle in a semicircle, and the properties of a cyclic quadrilateral - and uses them for angle chasing.

sections.heading: Central and inscribed angles
bullets: A central angle has its vertex at the centre O and its arms are radii; angle AOB is the central angle standing on arc AB.
An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle and its arms are chords; angle APB is the inscribed angle standing on arc AB from a point P on the remaining arc.
A chord splits a circle into a minor and a major arc, and the interior into a minor and a major segment; a diameter gives two semicircles.
The angle subtended by an arc at a point is the angle between the two lines from that point to the ends of the arc.

sections.heading: The Angle-at-Centre theorem
bullets: The angle an arc subtends at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining circle: angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.
Proof: join P to O and extend; each of triangles OAP and OBP is isosceles (two radii), so each exterior angle at O is twice a base angle at P.
Adding the two exterior angles at O gives angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.
For a major arc, the reflex central angle is used and the doubling relation still holds.

sections.heading: Angles in the same segment
bullets: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal: if P and Q lie on the same arc over chord AB then angle APB = angle AQB.
The reason: each inscribed angle is half of the SAME central angle AOB, so they are equal.
Converse: if AB subtends equal angles at P and Q on the same side of AB, the four points are concyclic.
This converse is the usual test for showing four points lie on one circle.

sections.heading: Angle in a semicircle
bullets: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: if AB is a diameter and P is on the circle, angle APB = 90 degrees.
It is a special case of the Angle-at-Centre theorem: the diameter subtends 180 degrees at the centre, and the inscribed angle is half of that.
Converse: if angle APB = 90 degrees for a fixed segment AB, then P lies on the circle with AB as diameter.
Hence the hypotenuse of a right triangle is a diameter of its circumcircle, and its midpoint is the circumcentre.

sections.heading: Cyclic quadrilaterals
bullets: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle; its sides are chords.
Opposite angles are supplementary: angle A + angle C = 180 and angle B + angle D = 180.
If a side is produced, the exterior angle equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.
Converse: if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is supplementary, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

key_takeaways: A central angle has its vertex at the centre; an inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle - both may stand on the same arc.
Angle-at-Centre theorem: angle AOB = 2 x angle APB (centre angle is double the circumference angle on the same arc).
Angles in the same segment are equal, because each is half of the same central angle.
The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees, since the diameter subtends 180 degrees at the centre.
In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are supplementary and the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
The converses of these results are the standard tests for concyclic points and cyclic quadrilaterals.
Angle chasing combines the circle theorems with the triangle angle-sum (180 degrees) and the isosceles property of radii.

glossary.definition: A line segment joining two points on a circle. A chord divides the circle into two arcs and the interior into two segments.
A chord passing through the centre; the longest chord, equal to twice the radius. It cuts the circle into two semicircles.
A part of a circle between two of its points. The shorter one is the minor arc and the longer one is the major arc.
A region of the interior bounded by a chord and one of the two arcs it cuts off - either the minor segment or the major segment.
Either half of a circle cut off by a diameter; the arc of a semicircle subtends 180 degrees at the centre.
An angle whose vertex is at the centre of the circle and whose arms are radii; angle AOB standing on arc AB.
An angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose arms are chords; angle APB subtended by arc AB at a point P on the remaining circle.
The angle formed at a point by the two lines drawn from that point to the two endpoints of the arc (or chord).
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining circle.
Inscribed angles standing on the same chord from points on the same arc; they are all equal.
The inscribed angle standing on a diameter; it is always a right angle (90 degrees).
A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on one circle. Its opposite angles are supplementary.
Points that all lie on a single circle. Four points are concyclic when they satisfy the same-segment or opposite-angle test.
Two angles whose measures add up to 180 degrees, as with the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.
The angle formed when a side of a cyclic quadrilateral is produced; it equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Angles in a Circle (NIOS)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw a rough figure where helpful, state the circle theorem you use, and show all angle calculations. Angles are in degrees.

questions.question: State the Angle-at-Centre theorem and use it: if an arc AB subtends a central angle AOB = 110 degrees, find the angle APB it subtends at a point P on the major arc.
questions.answer:
Theorem: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle, i.e. angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.
Here angle AOB = 110 degrees, so angle APB = (1/2) x 110 = 55 degrees.
questions.explanation: State the theorem, then halve the central angle.

questions.question: AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O and C is a point on the circle. If angle CAB = 32 degrees, find angle ABC. Justify each step.
questions.answer:
Since AB is a diameter, angle ACB is the angle in a semicircle, so angle ACB = 90 degrees.
In triangle ABC the three angles sum to 180 degrees: angle CAB + angle ACB + angle ABC = 180.
So 32 + 90 + angle ABC = 180, giving angle ABC = 180 - 122 = 58 degrees.
questions.explanation: Angle in a semicircle = 90 degrees, then use the triangle angle-sum.

questions.question: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 88 degrees and angle B = 96 degrees. Find angle C and angle D, stating the property used.
questions.answer:
In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180 degrees).
angle C = 180 - angle A = 180 - 88 = 92 degrees.
angle D = 180 - angle B = 180 - 96 = 84 degrees.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees.

questions.question: Points P and Q lie on the major arc of a circle over chord AB. Explain why angle APB = angle AQB, and if angle APB = 41 degrees, state angle AQB.
questions.answer:
Both angle APB and angle AQB are inscribed angles standing on the same chord AB from points on the same arc, so they are angles in the same segment. By the Angle-at-Centre theorem each equals half of the same central angle AOB, hence they are equal.
Therefore angle AQB = angle APB = 41 degrees.
questions.explanation: Angles in the same segment are equal because each is half the same central angle.

questions.question: Prove the Angle-at-Centre theorem: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
questions.answer:
Let O be the centre and let arc AB subtend angle AOB at O and angle APB at a point P on the major arc. Join PO and produce it to a point Q beyond O, so line PQ passes through O.
In triangle OAP, OA = OP (both radii), so it is isosceles and angle OAP = angle OPA. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so exterior angle AOQ = angle OAP + angle OPA = 2 x angle OPA.
Similarly in triangle OBP, OB = OP (radii), so angle OBP = angle OPB, and exterior angle BOQ = 2 x angle OPB.
Adding: angle AOQ + angle BOQ = 2(angle OPA + angle OPB), that is angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.
Hence the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. (For a major arc the reflex angle at the centre is used and the same relation holds.)
questions.explanation: Construction through O, isosceles radii, exterior-angle property, then add.

questions.question: One side AB of a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD is produced to E. If angle ADC = 76 degrees, find the exterior angle CBE. Justify.
questions.answer:
The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.
Here the exterior angle at B (angle CBE, formed by producing AB) equals the interior opposite angle ADC.
So angle CBE = angle ADC = 76 degrees.
questions.explanation: Exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral = interior opposite angle.

questions.question: A chord AB subtends an angle of 25 degrees at a point on the major arc. Find (a) the central angle AOB, and (b) the angle it subtends at a point on the minor arc.
questions.answer:
(a) By the Angle-at-Centre theorem, central angle AOB = 2 x 25 = 50 degrees (the non-reflex angle AOB on the minor-arc side).
(b) A point on the MINOR arc lies in the other segment. That angle and the 25 degrees are opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral formed, so they are supplementary: angle = 180 - 25 = 155 degrees.
questions.explanation: Double for the centre; supplementary for the opposite segment.

questions.question: State the converse of the 'angle in a semicircle' theorem and explain what it tells us about the circumcircle of a right-angled triangle.
questions.answer:
Converse: if a segment AB subtends a right angle (90 degrees) at a point P, then P lies on the circle having AB as diameter.
Consequence for a right triangle: the right angle 'sees' the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is a diameter of the triangle's circumscribed circle. The midpoint of the hypotenuse is therefore the circumcentre and is equidistant from all three vertices (each distance equals half the hypotenuse).
questions.explanation: Right angle -> point on circle with hypotenuse as diameter; midpoint of hypotenuse is circumcentre.

questions.question: In a circle with centre O, points A, B, C lie on the circle. Angle BOC = 130 degrees (central angle on minor arc BC). Find angle BAC where A is on the major arc, and hence angle OBC.
questions.answer:
By the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angle BAC = (1/2) x angle BOC = (1/2) x 130 = 65 degrees.
Triangle OBC is isosceles since OB = OC (radii), so its base angles are equal: angle OBC = angle OCB. The three angles sum to 180, so 2 x angle OBC = 180 - 130 = 50, giving angle OBC = 25 degrees.
questions.explanation: Halve the central angle for angle BAC; use isosceles triangle OBC for angle OBC.

questions.question: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Prove that a pair of opposite angles sums to 180 degrees, and use it to find angle B and angle D when angle B = (2x + 4) degrees and angle D = (3x + 6) degrees.
questions.answer:
Proof: Let O be the centre. Angle A is the inscribed angle standing on arc BCD, so angle A = (1/2)(central angle on arc BCD). Angle C stands on the other arc BAD, so angle C = (1/2)(central angle on arc BAD). The two central angles together make a complete angle of 360 degrees, so angle A + angle C = (1/2)(360) = 180 degrees. The same argument gives angle B + angle D = 180 degrees.
Application: angle B + angle D = 180, so (2x + 4) + (3x + 6) = 180, giving 5x + 10 = 180, 5x = 170, x = 34.
Then angle B = 2(34) + 4 = 72 degrees and angle D = 3(34) + 6 = 108 degrees. (Check: 72 + 108 = 180.)
questions.explanation: Prove opposite angles supplementary via central angles summing to 360, then solve the linear equation.

questions.explanation: angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.

questions.question: If the central angle is 130 degrees, the inscribed angle on the same arc is ____ degrees.
If an inscribed angle is 39 degrees, the central angle on the same arc is ____ degrees.

questions.explanation: On one circle.

questions.question: In triangle OAB with OA = OB (radii) and angle AOB = 100 degrees, each base angle is ____ degrees.
Define a central angle and an inscribed angle of a circle.
questions.answer: A central angle is an angle whose vertex is at the centre O of the circle and whose two arms are radii; angle AOB standing on arc AB is a central angle. An inscribed angle is an angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose two arms are chords; angle APB, with P a point on the remaining arc, is the inscribed angle on arc AB.
questions.explanation: Vertex position and arms distinguish them.

questions.question: Explain the terms minor arc, major arc, and segment of a circle.
questions.answer: Any chord that is not a diameter divides a circle into two arcs: the shorter is the MINOR arc and the longer is the MAJOR arc. The chord also divides the interior into two regions called SEGMENTS - the minor segment (on the minor-arc side) and the major segment (on the major-arc side). A diameter divides the circle into two equal semicircles.
questions.explanation: Arcs by length; segments by chord + arc.

questions.question: State the Angle-at-Centre theorem and explain, in one line, why the proof needs the isosceles property of radii.
questions.answer: Theorem: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining circle (angle AOB = 2 x angle APB). The proof joins P through O; because OA = OP and OB = OP are radii, triangles OAP and OBP are isosceles, so each base angle at P equals the corresponding base angle, letting each exterior angle at O be twice a base angle.
questions.explanation: Isosceles radii make the exterior angle double a base angle.

questions.question: A central angle AOB = 84 degrees. Find the inscribed angle on the same arc, and the central angle if the inscribed angle were 84 degrees instead.
questions.answer: Inscribed angle on the same arc = (1/2) x 84 = 42 degrees. If instead the inscribed angle were 84 degrees, the central angle would be 2 x 84 = 168 degrees.
questions.explanation: Halve, then double.

questions.question: In a circle with centre O, angle AOB = 108 degrees (minor arc AB). Find (a) the inscribed angle APB on the major arc and (b) the inscribed angle on the minor arc.
questions.answer: (a) angle APB = (1/2) x 108 = 54 degrees. (b) A point on the minor arc lies in the opposite segment; that angle is supplementary to 54, so it is 180 - 54 = 126 degrees.
questions.explanation: Half for major arc; supplement for the other segment.

questions.question: Prove that angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
questions.answer: Let chord AB cut off a segment, and let P and Q be two points on the same arc. Let O be the centre. By the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angle AOB = 2 x angle APB and also angle AOB = 2 x angle AQB, since both inscribed angles stand on the same arc AB. Therefore 2 x angle APB = 2 x angle AQB, giving angle APB = angle AQB. Hence angles in the same segment are equal.
questions.explanation: Both inscribed angles are half the same central angle.

questions.question: P and Q lie on the same arc over chord AB. If angle APB = (3x) degrees and angle AQB = (x + 50) degrees, find x and the common angle.
questions.answer: Angles in the same segment are equal, so 3x = x + 50, giving 2x = 50, x = 25. The common angle = 3x = 75 degrees (check: x + 50 = 75).
questions.explanation: Set the two equal and solve.

questions.question: Explain why the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
questions.answer: If AB is a diameter, then A, O, B are collinear, so the arc AB subtends a straight angle of 180 degrees at the centre O. For any point P on the circle, angle APB is the inscribed angle on this arc and, by the Angle-at-Centre theorem, equals half the central angle: angle APB = (1/2)(180) = 90 degrees. Hence the angle in a semicircle is always a right angle.
questions.explanation: Diameter subtends 180 at centre; half is 90.

questions.question: AB is a diameter of a circle and C is a point on it with angle BAC = 42 degrees. Find angle ABC and angle ACB.
questions.answer: Since AB is a diameter, angle ACB = 90 degrees (angle in a semicircle). In triangle ABC, angle BAC + angle ABC + angle ACB = 180, so 42 + angle ABC + 90 = 180, giving angle ABC = 48 degrees.
questions.explanation: Right angle at C, then triangle angle-sum.

questions.question: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 100 degrees and angle B = 75 degrees. Find angle C and angle D.
questions.answer: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary. angle C = 180 - angle A = 180 - 100 = 80 degrees. angle D = 180 - angle B = 180 - 75 = 105 degrees.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles sum to 180.

questions.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = (2x + 15) degrees and angle C = (3x) degrees. Find x and both angles.
questions.answer: Opposite angles are supplementary: (2x + 15) + 3x = 180, so 5x + 15 = 180, 5x = 165, x = 33. Then angle A = 2(33) + 15 = 81 degrees and angle C = 3(33) = 99 degrees (check: 81 + 99 = 180).
questions.explanation: Sum of opposite angles = 180; solve.

questions.question: Prove that the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
questions.answer: Let ABCD be cyclic and produce side AB to E. Angle CBE and angle ABC form a linear pair, so angle CBE = 180 - angle ABC. Also, ABCD is cyclic so opposite angles are supplementary: angle ABC + angle ADC = 180, hence angle ADC = 180 - angle ABC. Comparing, angle CBE = angle ADC, i.e. the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
questions.explanation: Linear pair plus opposite-angles-supplementary.

questions.question: O is the centre of a circle; A and B are on it with angle OAB = 35 degrees. Find angle AOB and the inscribed angle ACB (C on major arc).
questions.answer: Triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB, radii), so angle OBA = angle OAB = 35 degrees, and angle AOB = 180 - 35 - 35 = 110 degrees. The inscribed angle on the same arc is angle ACB = (1/2) x 110 = 55 degrees.
questions.explanation: Isosceles triangle for centre angle, then halve.

questions.question: In a circle, AB is a diameter and C, D are points on the same side with angle ACB and angle ADB. Explain their measures, and if angle DAB = 20 degrees find angle DBA.
questions.answer: Since AB is a diameter, both angle ACB and angle ADB are angles in a semicircle, so each equals 90 degrees. In right triangle ADB, angle ADB = 90, so angle DAB + angle DBA = 90; with angle DAB = 20, angle DBA = 90 - 20 = 70 degrees.
questions.explanation: Both are 90 (semicircle); complementary acute angles in the right triangle.

questions.question: State the converse of the 'angles in the same segment' theorem and say what it is used to prove.
questions.answer: Converse: if a line segment AB subtends equal angles at two points P and Q lying on the same side of AB, then the four points A, B, P, Q are concyclic (lie on one circle). It is used as a test to prove that four given points lie on a common circle.
questions.explanation: Equal angles on the same side -> concyclic.

questions.question: A wall clock is modelled as a circle with centre O. The tip of the minute hand at 12 is point A and at 4 is point B, so the central angle AOB = 120 degrees. A ladybird sits at a point P on the far (major) arc between B and A. (a) What is the inscribed angle APB? (b) What kind of angle is angle AOB? (c) If the ladybird moves to another point Q on the same arc, what is angle AQB? (d) Which theorem justifies your answers to (a) and (c)?
questions.answer: (a) angle APB = (1/2) x angle AOB = (1/2) x 120 = 60 degrees. (b) angle AOB is a central angle (vertex at the centre O, arms are radii). (c) angle AQB = 60 degrees, the same as at P, because P and Q lie on the same arc/segment. (d) The Angle-at-Centre theorem (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference) gives (a); its corollary, angles in the same segment are equal, gives (c).
questions.explanation: Halve the central angle; same-segment gives equal angles.

questions.question: A carpenter draws a circle and marks a diameter AB. She then marks a point C anywhere on the circle and joins CA and CB to form triangle ABC. (a) What is the measure of angle ACB, and why? (b) If angle CAB = 55 degrees, find angle CBA. (c) What special name is given to triangle ABC? (d) Where is the circumcentre of this triangle located?
questions.answer: (a) angle ACB = 90 degrees, because it is the angle in a semicircle (AB is a diameter, subtending 180 degrees at the centre, so the inscribed angle is half = 90). (b) In triangle ABC, angles sum to 180: 55 + 90 + angle CBA = 180, so angle CBA = 35 degrees. (c) Triangle ABC is a right-angled triangle (right angle at C). (d) The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse AB (the centre O of the circle).
questions.explanation: Angle in a semicircle = 90; triangle angle-sum; hypotenuse is diameter.

questions.question: In a cyclic quadrilateral PQRS inscribed in a circle, angle P = 95 degrees and angle Q = 70 degrees. Side PQ is produced to a point T. (a) Find angle R. (b) Find angle S. (c) State the property relating angle P and angle R. (d) Find the exterior angle RQT.
questions.answer: (a) Opposite angles are supplementary: angle R = 180 - angle P = 180 - 95 = 85 degrees. (b) angle S = 180 - angle Q = 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. (c) angle P and angle R are opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral, so they are supplementary (sum 180 degrees). (d) The exterior angle at Q, angle RQT, equals the interior opposite angle P, so angle RQT = 95 degrees.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles supplementary; exterior = interior opposite.

questions.question: A student is proving the Angle-at-Centre theorem. She has a circle with centre O, an arc AB, a point P on the major arc, and she has drawn PO produced to Q. (a) Why is triangle OAP isosceles? (b) Express the exterior angle AOQ in terms of angle OPA. (c) Similarly express angle BOQ. (d) Combine these to complete the proof that angle AOB = 2 x angle APB.
questions.answer: (a) Triangle OAP is isosceles because OA and OP are both radii, so OA = OP; hence angle OAP = angle OPA. (b) The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the remote interior angles, so angle AOQ = angle OAP + angle OPA = 2 x angle OPA. (c) Similarly OB = OP (radii), so angle BOQ = 2 x angle OPB. (d) Adding: angle AOB = angle AOQ + angle BOQ = 2 x angle OPA + 2 x angle OPB = 2(angle OPA + angle OPB) = 2 x angle APB. This completes the proof.
questions.explanation: Isosceles radii, exterior-angle property, then add the two parts.

questions.question: Points A, B, C, D lie on a circle. Chord AB is fixed, and C and D lie on the same arc on one side of AB. It is found that angle ACB = angle ADB = 47 degrees. (a) What is the name for angles ACB and ADB? (b) Why are they equal? (c) If a new point E on the same arc is added, what is angle AEB? (d) What does the converse of this theorem let you conclude about four points that subtend equal angles?
questions.answer: (a) They are angles in the same segment (inscribed angles on chord AB from points on the same arc). (b) They are equal because each equals half of the same central angle AOB, by the Angle-at-Centre theorem. (c) angle AEB = 47 degrees, the same value, since E is on the same arc. (d) By the converse, if a segment subtends equal angles at points on the same side, those points are concyclic - so four such points lie on one circle.
questions.explanation: Same-segment angles equal; converse gives concyclicity.

questions.question: In a circle with centre O, AB is a chord and OA, OB are radii. It is given that angle AOB = 88 degrees, and C is a point on the major arc. (a) Find angle OAB. (b) Find the inscribed angle angle ACB. (c) A point D is taken on the minor arc; find angle ADB. (d) Verify that angle ACB and angle ADB are supplementary and explain why.
questions.answer: (a) Triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB radii), so angle OAB = angle OBA = (180 - 88)/2 = 46 degrees. (b) By the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angle ACB = (1/2) x angle AOB = (1/2) x 88 = 44 degrees. (c) D is on the minor arc, in the opposite segment; angle ADB = 180 - 44 = 136 degrees. (d) angle ACB + angle ADB = 44 + 136 = 180 degrees, so they are supplementary. This is because ACBD is a cyclic quadrilateral and C, D lie in different segments over the same chord AB, so the angles are supplementary (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral).
questions.explanation: Isosceles triangle, halve central angle, opposite segment supplementary.

questions.question: A semicircular window has its flat edge AB as the diameter (2.0 m long) with centre O. A decorative bar runs from A to a point C on the curved edge and another from C to B, meeting at C. (a) What is angle ACB? (b) What is the radius of the window? (c) If C is the midpoint of the arc, what are angle CAB and angle CBA? (d) State the theorem used in (a).
questions.answer: (a) angle ACB = 90 degrees, the angle in a semicircle. (b) Radius = half the diameter = 1.0 m. (c) If C is the midpoint of the arc, triangle ACB is right-angled and isosceles (CA = CB), so angle CAB = angle CBA = (180 - 90)/2 = 45 degrees each. (d) The angle-in-a-semicircle theorem (a special case of the Angle-at-Centre theorem).
questions.explanation: Right angle in a semicircle; isosceles split of the remaining 90.

questions.question: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which AB is a diameter of the circle. Given angle ADC = 130 degrees. (a) Find angle ABC. (b) Since AB is a diameter, what is angle ACB? (c) Find angle BAC if angle ABC is now known and C lies so that triangle ABC is right-angled at C. (d) Explain how two different circle theorems were used.
questions.answer: (a) Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so angle ABC = 180 - angle ADC = 180 - 130 = 50 degrees. (b) AB is a diameter, so angle ACB = 90 degrees (angle in a semicircle). (c) In right triangle ACB, angle BAC = 180 - 90 - angle ABC = 180 - 90 - 50 = 40 degrees. (d) The cyclic-quadrilateral opposite-angle property gave angle ABC; the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem gave angle ACB = 90, and the triangle angle-sum finished the chase.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles supplementary, then angle in a semicircle, then angle-sum.

questions.question: In a circle centred at O, an arc AB subtends a central angle angle AOB = (5x) degrees and an inscribed angle angle ACB = (2x + 6) degrees at a point C on the major arc. (a) Write the relation between angle AOB and angle ACB. (b) Form an equation and solve for x. (c) State angle AOB and angle ACB. (d) Verify your answer satisfies the Angle-at-Centre theorem.
questions.answer: (a) By the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angle AOB = 2 x angle ACB. (b) So 5x = 2(2x + 6), giving 5x = 4x + 12, hence x = 12. (c) angle AOB = 5x = 60 degrees and angle ACB = 2x + 6 = 30 degrees. (d) Check: 2 x angle ACB = 2 x 30 = 60 = angle AOB, so the Angle-at-Centre theorem is satisfied.
questions.explanation: Set central = 2 x inscribed, solve the linear equation, then verify.

questions.question: Three friends stand on the boundary of a circular field at points A, C and D, and a flag is at the centre O. Points A and B are ends of a chord. angle AOB = 140 degrees. (a) Find the angle angle ACB seen by the friend at C on the major arc. (b) What is angle OAB in triangle OAB? (c) If the friend at D is on the minor arc, what angle ADB does she see? (d) Add angle ACB and angle ADB and comment.
questions.answer: (a) angle ACB = (1/2) x angle AOB = (1/2) x 140 = 70 degrees. (b) Triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB radii), so angle OAB = (180 - 140)/2 = 20 degrees. (c) D on the minor arc is in the opposite segment, so angle ADB = 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. (d) angle ACB + angle ADB = 70 + 110 = 180 degrees; the two angles are supplementary because C and D are in opposite segments over the same chord (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral).
questions.explanation: Halve for C, isosceles for OAB, supplement for D.

questions.question: With reference to a chord PQ and a point R on the circle, explain what 'the angle subtended by PQ at R' means.
questions.answer: The angle subtended by chord PQ at the point R is the angle QRP formed at R by the two line segments RP and RQ drawn from R to the endpoints P and Q of the chord. As R moves along a fixed arc, this angle stays the same (angles in the same segment); when R is at the centre it becomes the central angle.
questions.explanation: It is the angle between the two lines from R to the chord's ends.

questions.question: How does a diameter differ from an ordinary chord? Give two points.
questions.answer: (1) A diameter passes through the centre of the circle, whereas a general chord need not. (2) A diameter is the longest chord and equals twice the radius, and it divides the circle into two equal semicircles, while an ordinary chord divides the circle into an unequal minor arc and major arc.
questions.explanation: Passes through centre; longest chord; equal semicircles.

questions.question: Why is the angle-in-a-semicircle result called a special case of the Angle-at-Centre theorem?
questions.answer: In the Angle-at-Centre theorem, angle AOB = 2 x angle APB. When AB is a diameter, the points A, O, B are collinear, so the central angle angle AOB is a straight angle of 180 degrees. Substituting gives angle APB = (1/2)(180) = 90 degrees. Thus the right angle in a semicircle is just the theorem applied to a central angle of 180 degrees.
questions.explanation: Put angle AOB = 180 into the theorem to get 90.

questions.question: The inscribed angle subtended by an arc is 27 degrees. Find the central angle subtended by the same arc.
questions.answer: By the Angle-at-Centre theorem the central angle is double the inscribed angle: central angle = 2 x 27 = 54 degrees.
questions.explanation: Double the inscribed angle.

questions.question: In a circle, the reflex angle AOB at the centre is 220 degrees. Find the inscribed angle APB where P lies on the MINOR arc.
questions.answer: When P is on the minor arc, the inscribed angle corresponds to the reflex central angle. So angle APB = (1/2) x 220 = 110 degrees.
questions.explanation: Half of the reflex central angle.

questions.question: Two points C and D lie on the same arc drawn on chord AB. angle ACB = 52 degrees. What is angle ADB and why?
questions.answer: angle ADB = 52 degrees. Both angle ACB and angle ADB are angles in the same segment standing on the same chord AB, and angles in the same segment are equal (each is half the same central angle).
questions.explanation: Same segment -> equal angles.

questions.question: A, B, C, D are four points such that angle ACB = angle ADB, with C and D on the same side of line AB. What can you conclude and by which result?
questions.answer: We can conclude that the four points A, B, C, D are concyclic (lie on a single circle). This follows from the CONVERSE of the 'angles in the same segment' theorem: if a segment AB subtends equal angles at two points on the same side of AB, those points and A, B lie on one circle.
questions.explanation: Converse of same-segment theorem gives concyclicity.

questions.question: AB is a diameter and P is on the circle. If angle PAB = 90 degrees is claimed, is it possible? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Since AB is a diameter, the right angle occurs at P (the point on the circle), i.e. angle APB = 90 degrees. The angle at A (angle PAB) is one of the two acute angles of the right triangle APB, so it must be less than 90 degrees. Hence angle PAB cannot be 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: The right angle is at the circumference point P, not at A.

questions.question: The hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is 13 cm. Find the radius of its circumscribed circle and locate the circumcentre.
questions.answer: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumscribed circle (converse of the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem). So the diameter is 13 cm and the radius is 13/2 = 6.5 cm. The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse is the diameter; radius = half of it.

questions.question: State two properties of a cyclic quadrilateral concerning its angles.
questions.answer: (1) The opposite angles are supplementary: they add up to 180 degrees. (2) If a side is produced, the exterior angle so formed equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles supplementary; exterior = interior opposite.

questions.question: In a cyclic quadrilateral, one angle is 3 times its opposite angle. Find both angles.
questions.answer: Let the smaller angle be x; its opposite is 3x. Opposite angles are supplementary: x + 3x = 180, so 4x = 180, x = 45. The two opposite angles are 45 degrees and 135 degrees.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles sum to 180; solve x + 3x = 180.

questions.question: A parallelogram is inscribed in a circle. What special quadrilateral must it be? Justify using cyclic-quadrilateral properties.
questions.answer: It must be a rectangle. In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal; in a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles are supplementary. So each pair of opposite angles is both equal and adds to 180, which forces each angle to be 90 degrees. A parallelogram with all right angles is a rectangle.
questions.explanation: Equal AND supplementary opposite angles force 90 degrees each.

questions.question: In a circle with centre O, angle ACB = 40 degrees is an inscribed angle on arc AB, and OA, OB are joined. Find angle OAB.
questions.answer: The central angle angle AOB = 2 x angle ACB = 2 x 40 = 80 degrees. Triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB, radii), so angle OAB = angle OBA = (180 - 80)/2 = 50 degrees.
questions.explanation: Double for the centre angle, then isosceles triangle.

questions.question: AB is a diameter of a circle; C and D are points on the circle on opposite sides of AB with angle CAB = 30 degrees and angle DAB = 40 degrees. Find angle ACB, angle ADB, and angle CBD.
questions.answer: Both C and D see the diameter AB, so angle ACB = 90 degrees and angle ADB = 90 degrees (angle in a semicircle). In right triangle ACB, angle ABC = 180 - 90 - 30 = 60 degrees. In right triangle ADB, angle ABD = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 degrees. Since C and D are on opposite sides of AB, angle CBD = angle ABC + angle ABD = 60 + 50 = 110 degrees.
questions.explanation: Both angles at C and D are 90; add the two base angles at B.

questions.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle DAB = 60 degrees and angle ABC = 80 degrees. A person claims angle BCD = 120 degrees and angle CDA = 100 degrees. Check the claim.
questions.answer: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary. angle BCD = 180 - angle DAB = 180 - 60 = 120 degrees, which matches. angle CDA = 180 - angle ABC = 180 - 80 = 100 degrees, which also matches. So the claim is correct.
questions.explanation: Verify each pair of opposite angles sums to 180.
